author: Felicia Anthonio
title: #KeepItOn @10: celebrating a decade of fighting internet shutdowns
content:
Internet shutdowns are widely viewed as an attack on human rights. But that wasn’t always the case. A decade ago, civil society groups joined forces to push back against deliberate network disruptions, and today, the resistance to shutdowns is stronger than ever. As Access Now and the #KeepItOn community mark the 10th anniversary of the #KeepItOn campaign in 2026, we’re reflecting on the path travelled so far — and the journey still to come as we continue to fight to #KeepItOn around the world.

Read on for a look at how the #KeepItOn campaign started, how it has evolved, and how you can join us to support and celebrate the work of the #KeepItOn coalition.

Ten years ago, there were no strong global norms condemning internet shutdowns. The groups fighting shutdowns were only loosely connected, and the lack of coordination made it difficult to get a global picture of the many harms people were experiencing — even as governments disconnected entire communities, disrupted business and daily life, undermined election integrity, exacerbated humanitarian crises, and attempted to hide grave human rights abuses and violations.

author: Amina Khan
title: #KeepItOn: authorities in Zambia must resist hitting the kill switch during upcoming elections
content:
Access Now and the #KeepItOn coalition — a global network of over 370 organizations from 106 countries working to end internet shutdowns, through an open letter , are urging Zambian authorities to ensure unfettered access to the internet throughout the upcoming elections.

As millions of people prepare to cast their votes on August 13, 2026, Access Now and the #KeepItOn coalition call on President Hakainde Hichilema to issue a directive to all relevant institutions, including the Zambia Information and Communications Technology Authority (ZICTA), the Ministry of Technology and Science, and all internet service providers (ISPs) operating in the country, to refrain from disrupting access to the internet and digital platforms and to ensure unrestricted access during the electoral cycle and beyond.

In June 2026 , the Ministry of Technology and Science assured the people of Zambia that the government will not deliberately shut down the internet during the upcoming elections. Access Now and the #KeepItOn coalition welcome this commitment and will be watching.

During the 2021 election, Zambian authorities flipped the kill switch , disrupting access to major social media platforms including Facebook, Twitter, and Instagram across the country. Similar disruptions were reported in 2020 and 2016 .

author: Aymen Zaghdoudi
title: The game is up: how MENA’s social media regulations silence and control
content:
Imagine a basketball game where one team writes the rules, owns the court, and controls the referee. The crowd is silenced before tip-off, and the opposing players are warned that every play could end the match. That is not a free and fair game, it is a performance of control. The new wave of social media regulations in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region works just like that.




Two decades after MENA governments responded to the rise of social media with a 

first wave of cybercrime legislations

, they are once again seeking to expand their power over what people say and do online. Over the past three years, a number of governments have increased their control over social media platforms by widening the scope of their 

cybercrime laws

 or introducing dedicated 

social media laws

. These 

draft laws

 are purportedly inspired by the 

EU’s Digital Services Act

 (DSA), but 

open up risks

 that have no parallel in European democracies. As we will explain, transplanting DSA-inspired regulations can turn a framework meant to protect people’s rights into a sophisticated instrument for state censorship and control. It also poses 

new challenges for social media companies

 operating in authoritarian contexts — making it all the more important that they meet their responsibilities to respect human rights.

author: Giulio Coppi
title: Not AI for Good
content:
July 15 @ 1:00 pm – 2:00 pm CEST

This civil society-led counter-event to the AI for Good Global Summit takes a critical look at the overhyped role of AI in solving humanity’s long-standing problems, and at the UN’s ongoing partnerships with tech companies increasingly implicated in human rights abuses, violence, and armed conflict.

Building on the recent joint civil society statement on AI in warfare , launched by Access Now and Amnesty International — backed by over 350 signatories — and Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect’s joint webinar on Emerging Approaches to the Protection of Civilians in the Age of AI , Not AI for Good calls for an urgent rethinking of the tech-solutionist vision currently driving the humanitarian sector. It also examines the growing role of tech companies as defense contractors, and their part in exacerbating the very crises the humanitarian sector seeks to address.

Join us for an off-the-cuff and frank discussion about what goes unsaid at the AI for Good Summit ,  and to explore pathways toward a more just and fair humanitarian tech ecosystem.
